title: Refinement and Pilot Testing of a Computerized Distress Tolerance Intervention with Just-In-Time Text Message Reminders for Cannabis Use Disorder
text:
Project Narrative. This project is relevant to public health because it represents a novel, targeted harm
reduction approach to the treatment of Cannabis Use Disorder, a major public health concern in the era of
increasing cannabis legalization. This study aims to evaluate the effect of a one-session computerized distress
tolerance intervention with just-in-time text message support on distress tolerance, stress-related cannabis use
motivation, disordered cannabis use, and psychosocial functioning, representing a highly portable, low-cost
solution to the problem of Cannabis Use Disorder.

title: Exploring the interplay of viral genomic RNA structure and protein biochemistry in coronavirus replication
text:
Coronaviruses are a global threat to human and animal health, being responsible for roughly 15-30% of common
colds and causing several outbreaks and even a pandemic over the past twenty years. The proposed project
seeks to elucidate the biomolecular interactions driving key molecular processes of the coronavirus life cycle,
including viral genome replication and packaging. With an approach rooted in biochemistry and structural biology,
this project will yield insights into coronavirus RNA-protein interactions that in turn will inform the design of
broadly-acting antivirals and vaccines.

title: Project 2: Determinants of Response and Resistance to DNA-Damaging Radiation Plus Immunotherapy Combinations in Triple Negative Breast Cancer
text:
Project 2: Determinants of Response and Resistance to DNA-Damaging Radiation Plus Immunotherapy
Combinations in Triple Negative Breast Cancer – PROJECT NARRATIVE
Immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) combined with chemotherapy has transformed outcomes for patients with
early-stage triple negative breast cancer (TNBC). Breast SPORE Project 2 will identify biomarkers that can
inform the optimal use of new combinations of ICI with targeted radiation therapy and/or neoantigen
vaccination in early stage TNBC.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Thoracic Aortic Disease Screening and Gene Discovery
text:
Thoracic aortic dissections, a leading cause of premature death particularly in those with heritable thoracic aortic
disease (HTAD), are entirely preventable if at-risk individuals are identified early and undergo surgical repair.
Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning approaches, represents an ideal method
for identifying these individuals and gaining insights into the largely undefined genetic basis of aortic disease. In
this proposal, I aim to (1) develop an AI-based facial feature screening tool by leveraging images from the
Montalcino Aortic Consortium patient registry, and (2) integrate machine learning techniques and evolutionary
principles to identify novel genetic drivers of HTAD using genomic-scale data from diverse cohorts.

title: Predicting Pouchitis in Inflammatory Bowel Disease Through Immune-Epithelial Profiling
text:
Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) who undergo ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) are at high
risk of developing pouchitis, a common inflammatory complication of the surgically constructed ileal pouch. The
underlying mechanisms that predispose to or trigger pouchitis remain poorly defined, representing a critical gap
in our understanding of IBD pathogenesis. This project seeks to elucidate how pre-existing immune dysregulation
in the ileum contributes to epithelial dysfunction and subsequent pouch inflammation, leveraging longitudinal
profiling and patient-derived organoid models to identify predictive immune, epithelial, and microbial biomarkers
that may inform prevention and treatment strategies.

title: Analytics Core
text: ANALYTIC CORE Revised Abstract The Analytic Core will process and harmonize multi-omics and multimodal endophenotype data, and provide advanced computational systems biology methods and frameworks for data integration and analysis for the entire project. Our multidisciplinary team has substantial expertise in multi-omics data analysis, data harmonization, computational method development, multi-omics data integration, genetic association analysis, neuroimaging analysis, data visualization, biostatistics, and network analysis. The Core will support collaborative work of the U19 project by providing processed multi-omics and multimodal phenotype data and enhancing the interoperability of analysis methods and pipelines. Furthermore, the Core will work closely with the Administrative Core to curate and share newly generated data and to provide documentation of data processing for public access. The overall goal of the U19 is to identify and validate centrally-linked longitudinal peripheral biomarkers of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) in multi-ethnic populations by integrating longitudinal multi-omics and multimodal phenotypes from eight independent cohorts. To achieve this goal, harmonized high-quality processed data and advanced computational and systems biology methods and pipelines for data analysis are critical to the entire project. First, the Analytic Core will provide high-quality and harmonized high-throughput multi-omics data from blood and brain tissue and multimodal neuroimaging, cognitive and postmortem neuropathology data. This data will permit analyses connecting peripheral and central changes within and across clinical, community-based and multi-ethnic cohorts and samples. The Core will also implement and provide advanced computational, systems biology frameworks for high-dimensional data analysis, enabling investigators from all three projects to perform data integration and analysis. To this end, the Analytic Core will be comprised of five teams: Omics, Imaging, Clinical, Neuropathology, and Computational and Systems Biology teams. The Analytic Core will focus on new data processing and integrative analysis framework development of longitudinal multi-omics data in relation to longitudinal multimodal endophenotypes. In Aim 1, we will assemble and provide state-of-the-art pipelines for processing high-dimensional multi-omics from blood and brain tissue and multimodal neuroimaging data, as well as clinical, cognition and neuropathology phenotypes for all projects. In Aim 2, we will implement and provide advanced multi-omics and multimodal endophenotype data integration and analysis approaches and pipelines for the entire project, which include but not limited to (1) novel systems biology and deep learning platforms for identification of blood molecular signatures that are associated with molecular signatures in the brain; (2) network-guided integrative analysis methods for multi-omics data integration to predict disease progression; and (3) an advanced system for query, analysis, and visualization in systems biology. The Core will work closely with the other Cores and Projects to enable analysis of multi-omics and AD phenome data for each components’ specific needs.

title: Advancing One Health Data Capture at the Point of Zoonotic Spillover in the Congo Basin Forest Perimeter
text: This project will develop a scalable One Health mHealth platform that will elevate public health professionals’ ability to monitor human and animal health in remote rural settings in real-time, enabling more accurate investigations of potential zoonotic spillover events.

title: Cellular Imaging Core
text: Cellular Imaging Core Advanced cellular microscopy is a powerful tool for biological research and has an important role to play in the study of disease pathogenesis, which may translate eventually to novel treatment approaches for rheumatic diseases. Imaging technology has evolved rapidly over the last decade leading to improvements in resolution, sensitivity and speed which have created fundamentally new opportunities for studying processes across many orders of magnitude and in real-time in living cells and animals. At the same time, the costs of increasingly sophisticated equipment are substantial and the expertise to efficiently use, maintain, and develop this equipment is not common in most labs. There is therefore a significant gap between the availability of these powerful tools and the ability of investigators to access and use them efficiently. The Cellular Imaging Core (CIC) was originally created in response to feedback from Washington University Rheumatic Diseases Research Resource-based Center (WU-RDRRC) members to leverage the significant institutional investment in the newly created Washington University Center for Cellular Imaging (WUCCI) and provide an integrated approach to investigate the structure and dynamic behavior of cells and tissues in rheumatic disease-related model systems. The overall objective of the core is to provide access to and technical support in using advanced cellular microscopy tools to accelerate the pace, expand the scope, and improve efficiency of rheumatic diseases research. The core services meet the unique requirements of numerous investigators over a wide range of basic and translational research, attracting new investigators into rheumatic diseases research areas. Importantly the users benefit from the in-depth technical expertise of the Core Director and technical staff in the time spent in consultation for experimental design and interpretation of data. During the past funding cycle, the core served 28 WU-RDRRC investigator research laboratories, who expensed $520,699 in core recharges, which represented approximately 12% of all WUCCI activity. Fourteen WU-RDRRC investigator laboratories received micro-grant funding through the WU- RDRRC Imaging Core Scholarship program, 5 of which were junior faculty members. Given the broad usage of core over the past funding cycle, and the establishment of new imaging technologies (e.g. cryoEM and lattice lightsheet), sample preparation services (e.g. tissue clearing), and analysis approaches (e.g. AI-based IHC and IF image analysis), it is anticipated that requests for CIC services will continue to be robust given the overwhelming need for advanced microscopic imaging and image analysis approaches, thus accelerating the research endeavors of WU-RDRRC members throughout the next funding cycle.

title: Epilepsy and Neurodevelopmental Risk Stratification in Very Preterm Infants with Intraventricular Hemorrhage
text:
Preterm infants with intraventricular hemorrhage are at high risk of developing childhood epilepsy and may
provide important insights into epilepsy risk stratification if studied early. This study will capture high-density EEG
data from preterm infants with intraventricular hemorrhage during a critical period before epilepsy develops to
compare to both early epilepsy and developmental outcomes. The goal of this study is to identify predictive
biomarkers directly translatable to future clinical screening and interventions which prevent epilepsy in preterm
infants and others at risk.

title: Investigate the mechanisms underlying microRNA-146a activity in regulation of foreign body response to biomaterials
text:
Mortality and Morbidity in biomaterial and medical device-induced foreign body response (FBR) are very
high and are directly related to the development of inflammation and fibrosis in affected organs/tissues.
The results of this proposal promise to define the role of microRNA-146a in the pathogenesis of FBR,
and may lead to novel and effective therapeutics for FBR and other fibrotic disorders.

title: Detecting Malignancy and Treatment Response in NF1-Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors through cfDNA Fragmentomics
text:
This research will develop a noninvasive cell-free DNA (cfDNA) blood test to detect and monitor malignant
transformation in individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)-associated peripheral nerve sheath tumors. By
integrating cfDNA fragmentomic and epigenomic patterns into a malignancy risk score and testing it in preclinical
patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models, this work aims to identify malignant peripheral nerve sheath
tumors (MPNSTs) earlier and track response to targeted therapies. In the long term, the findings could enable
earlier intervention and more precise treatment decisions, improving survival and quality of life for people living
with NF1 and related hereditary cancer syndromes.

title: RNA Sequencing and Data Analysis Core
text:
The RNA Sequencing and Data Analysis Core will complete all high-throughput
sequencing, mass spectrometry analysis of RNA modification services and downstream
informatics and requested biostatistics to serve the needs of the P01 program. This includes
resources and expertise to perform a variety of experiments and state-of-the-art methods for
multi-omics analysis. Our core will also integrate multi-omics data to provide a comprehensive
understanding of extracellular RNA biogenesis and function in colorectal cancer.

title: LNP-associated inflammation: Identifying the mechanisms and reengineering LNPs to be non-inflammatory
text:
RNA loaded into lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have been given to >1 billion patients, and are therefore being
developed by industry for diverse diseases. However, we showed that LNPs can induce inflammation, or
worsen pre-existing inflammation. In this grant, we will identify the mechanisms of LNP-associated
inflammation (LAI) (Aim 1), and then engineer non-inflammatory LNPs (Aim 2), thus making RNA-LNPs much
safer, more effective, and able to help a broader array of patients.

title: Modeling Substance Abuse via a Behavioral Foundation Model Trained on Large-Scale Survey Data
text:
Substance use disorders impose significant public health and socioeconomic burdens, yet current
epidemiological surveys remain underutilized due to the limitations of traditional analysis methods. This project
develops a novel behavioral foundation model that leverages large language models to “textualize” and transform
diverse survey data from NESARC-III, NSDUH, and UK Biobank into robust, quantitative representations for
precise risk prediction and intervention design. Open dissemination of our innovative tool will empower public
health practitioners to enhance early SUD detection, optimize survey instruments, and ultimately reduce the
societal impact of substance use disorders.

title: Computational Modeling Guided Ablation for Atrial Flutteris
text:
Atypical left atrial flutter seen after ablation for atrial fibrillation can be difficult to treat. Here we are going to
develop a generalized computational model, which can be personalized with left atrial geometry, scar pattern,
and mapping results. Such a model will enable virtual electrophysiology studies leading to the prediction of
ablation points to terminate all possible such flutter pathways.

title: Evaluating the impact of TP53 mutation on the epigenetic therapy viral mimicry response in the non- small cell lung cancer tumor
text:
Immunotherapy represents an important advance in lung cancer treatment, but responses are often short-lived, 
including in the ~50% of lung cancers with TP53 mutations. Epigenetic drugs activate tumor cell antiviral signaling, 
priming for immunotherapy responses. This project will investigate how TP53 mutations shape the immune response to 
epigenetic therapy in tumor cells and the surrounding microenvironment, offering insights into the therapeutic potential 
of this combination approach in lung cancer.

title: Pharmacomicrobiomics: The Frontier of Interindividual Variability in Drug Response
text: The gut microbiome contributes to interindividual variability in drug responses, including efficacy and toxicity. By studying bacterial drug metabolism, we will develop strategies to predict and pre- vent drug-induced injury and reduce medication side effects, thus promoting public health. This research program will utilize human samples to understand how the microbiome alters drug re- sponse, thereby delivering on the promise of precision medicine for all.

title: Dissecting the transcription factor networks controlling fetal T-lineage differentiation
text:
The first wave of thymocyte differentiation in the fetal thymus proceeds rapidly and gives rise to specific
lineages of innate lymphocytes and innate-like T cells that are not generated by any subsequent wave of
development. Based on my preliminary data, I hypothesize that these populations arise from a dedicated
precursor cell in the fetal thymus that is using a unique differentiation program. In this proposal, I aim to test
test this hypothesis through fate mapping and perturbation studies to construct a full lineage hierarchy of fetal
thymocyte differentiation and the gene regulatory networks that govern it.

title: Linking substance use genetics to circadian function using high-throughput genomics
text:
Human genome wide association studies have found hundreds of loci that influence the predisposition to
addiction behavior, sleep behavior, or both. Although circadian rhythms have been tightly linked to addiction
and sleep, limitations in studying humans directly have led to difficulties in elucidating how differences in
genetics lead to differences in circadian gene regulation and addiction behavior. Here, we overcome those
limitations by combining high throughput genomic experiments in mice across times of day with predictions
across the human genome made by machine learning models.

title: Clinical Translation of a Urine-Based Biomarker for the Detection of Residual Disease in Radical Cystectomy Candidates
text:
About 25,000 patients per year are candidates for radical cystectomy, the surgical removal of their bladder and
associated structures with subsequent urinary diversion, for treatment of bladder cancer. In 40% of cases who
are treated with standard of care preoperative chemotherapy, the surgically removed bladder has no evidence
of cancer, meaning that bladder removal may have been safely avoided. This project will validate a test that
sequences DNA from the patient’s urine to detect any remaining cancer after chemotherapy, and if the test is
validated, it will be used in the future for clinical trials to evaluate the safety of biomarker-directed decision making
to avoid bladder surgery with careful follow-up monitoring in case the tumor recurs.
